proof.claim:
A controller that loses authority must never regain it by waking up.

THE FAULT. SIGSTOP the controller holding the leadership lease. Its lease is
not renewed, so it expires; another controller wins the election and changes
desired state. Then SIGCONT the original process.

    controller A holds the lease, instance 73781e90…
          ↓  SIGSTOP  — process frozen, memory intact
    lease expires, key disappears
          ↓
    controller B wins the election, becomes leader
          ↓
    B mutates desired state
          ↓  SIGCONT  — A wakes with perfectly coherent pre-freeze memory

WHY SIGKILL CANNOT REACH THIS. A killed process loses its memory and comes
back as a new instance that must re-elect from scratch — the safe path, and the
only one the existing crash scenarios exercise. A STOPPED process keeps every
byte: it wakes up still believing it is leader, still holding what it thinks is
a valid lease, mid-way through whatever it was doing. Every existing crash
drill tests that leader election WORKS. This tests something strictly harder:

    is losing authority IRREVERSIBLE for the instance that lost it?

network-partition-fencing attacks the spatial side of that invariant — an
isolated node must be fenced. This attacks the temporal side, which is the
half that survives a working fencing implementation: A is not isolated when it
wakes. It can reach etcd, it can reach every service, and it has no local
evidence that anything happened. Only the cluster knows.

WHAT MUST HOLD. Exactly one leader, and it is not the resurrected instance.
The zombie's own instance UUID must not reappear as leader_instance, and the
desired state B wrote must survive untouched. A must either observe that its
lease is gone and stand down, or be refused by the generation guard — but from
outside, the requirement is simply that nothing it believed becomes true again.

A NOTE ON WHAT THIS CAN OBSERVE. Proving "A performed no externally visible
mutation" in full needs write attribution per authority instance. What is
observable here is: leadership did not return to A's instance, desired state
is byte-identical to what B wrote, no split-brain or drift findings appeared,
and the cluster stayed healthy. Those are consequences of correct fencing
rather than the fencing itself, and the scenario says so rather than
overclaiming.
